assumptions.summary: Policy interventions are assumed to affect the system immediately.
Unexpected incidents and extreme events are excluded.
Variables and coefficients are treated as stable over the modeled period.
Selected data sources are treated as authoritative.
ELA is used as the Juneau environmental state.
Annual visitors are treated with a logistic population analogy.
Hotel-tax revenue represents the economic state.
Twelve selected indicators represent three broad sustainability factors.
Cliff retreat, park attendance, and park revenue substitute for Big Sur environmental, tourist, and economic states.

context_sources.observation: The Summary names H, N, and T, then gives Juneau score, two sensitivity methods, and a Big Sur transfer score before the keywords.
The memo addresses the Juneau Tourist Council, names a daily cap and a 40-percent allocation, and ends as MCM Team #2503268.
Contents was checked for section order only and is not treated as author-language evidence.
Location-specific overtourism leads to a global generalization, three restated tasks, and a short Our Work bridge.
Figure 1 previews the workflow before Assumptions 1-2 begin the premise-rationale sequence.
Assumptions 3-4 close before Table 1 freezes the shared notation.
The authors explicitly reject listing everything and choose accurate, representative data for the H-N-T system.
Natural change, tourist pressure, and tax-funded conservation are each explained before Equation (1).
Logistic tourism and hotel-tax dynamics are introduced separately before integration.
The 2013 Blob year is excluded, remaining data are interpolated, and Equations (4)-(6) add intervention terms.
Three qualitative insights from projections precede an intervention iteration passage disclosed as AI-assisted on page 26.
Nine allocation patterns and eight policies are introduced before evaluation indicators.
Figure 6 and Table 4 complete the evaluation hierarchy before explicit indicator formulas.
Each formula is preceded by a prose rationale, but several printed exponents and subscripts are ambiguous.
Housing, noise, natural resources, energy, waste, and carbon scores are developed in sequence; ambiguous layouts remain flagged.
Tax, employment, cultural, and safety scores close the indicator system before parameter estimation.
Table 5 precedes four comparison matrices and Table 6 weight outcomes.
AHP weights and H-N-T comparisons lead to a worked feasible intervention example.
The paper reports allocation [0.15,0.10,0.35,0.10,0.30], policy [-3,3,4], score 0.6894, then baseline/model comparisons.
Morris plots are followed by a local partial-derivative discussion and a handoff to Table 7.
Figure 11 precedes Big Sur data-source selection and transfer setup.
Table 7 closes sensitivity before cliff-retreat data define the Big Sur environmental state.
The transferred ODE system precedes least-squares fitting, a normalized state, and score 0.32773 to 0.73563.
Four strengths precede two weaknesses: unexpected events and immediate-policy assumptions.
References were inspected for provenance but excluded from positive author-language evidence.
The disclosure identifies two ChatGPT-assisted passages; the report and those passages are excluded from positive author-language evidence.

source.title: Rebalancing Nature's Scale: A Model to Tame Overtourism

source_quality.summary: Twenty-one pages have extractable substantive text and five pages have explicit human visual recovery. Human information order, transitions, mechanism explanations, formula handoffs, result cadence, transfer, self-evaluation, and memo language are retained, while five source-furniture classes and two AI-assisted passages are excluded. Proxy validity, dimensions, fitting, feasibility, formula typography, AHP, sensitivity, transfer, implementation, and reproducibility remain incomplete.

task_reconstruction: Develop a sustainable-tourism model for Juneau with explicit optimized factors and constraints.
Show how additional tourism revenue can be allocated to sustainability measures and include drawbacks or tradeoffs.
Perform sensitivity analysis and identify influential factors.
Apply the model to another overtourism destination and explain location-specific changes.
Use the model to support less-visited attractions or more balanced tourism where applicable.
Write a memorandum to the Tourist Council of Juneau with policy measures and expected effects.

unresolved_questions.summary: Watermarks, QR blocks, Chinese publisher/footer material, Contents, references, and the AI-use report are not positive author-language evidence.
The intervention-strategy passage and the Notably introduction passage are explicitly disclosed as ChatGPT-assisted and must not seed human-style language rules.
ELA, annual tourist count, and hotel-tax revenue are narrow proxies for environmental, social, and economic conditions; construct validity is not established.
H, N, and T use different physical scales, yet the coupled terms and intervention vectors lack a complete dimensional analysis.
ELA change is attributed to tourist pressure and tax-funded restoration without a causal identification design or separation from climate drivers.
Tourist arrivals are treated as a logistic population although visitors are flows, seasonality is strong, and carrying capacity K is not independently justified.
The hotel-tax ODE does not explicitly include tax rates, lodging prices, collection lags, cruise visitors, or non-tourism revenue.
Policy effects omega_H, omega_N, and omega_T are added directly to state derivatives without documented units or a reproducible policy-to-coefficient mapping.
The 2013 Blob observation is removed and remaining years interpolated, but the exclusion rule, interpolation method, sensitivity, and retained sample size are not fully documented.
Nonlinear least squares is named without complete input data, starting values, bounds, residual diagnostics, confidence intervals, or holdout validation.
Figures 3, 4, and 8 show fitted behavior, but visual agreement is not a substitute for residual, predictive, and out-of-sample checks.
Nine allocation arrays do not establish coverage or optimality of the five-dimensional allocation simplex.
Eight policy vectors and the selected [-3,3,4] code lack a fully auditable mapping from integers to implementable policy magnitudes.
Allocation shares are optimized without a clearly frozen total budget, feasibility constraints, legal restrictions, or implementation costs.
The paper proposes iterative policy feedback but does not specify observation intervals, triggers, controller stability, delay, or rollback.
Several evaluation indicators reuse N and T, creating potential double counting that AHP weights do not remove.
Benefit and cost indicators are mixed; direction, clipping, and bounds are not consistently documented.
Equation (7) contains visually unstable arrows, exponents, and mu subscripts; its exact algebra must be checked against the source before reuse.
Equation (9) has unclear exponent signs and parameter placement, so the asserted normalization range is not independently established.
Equation (14) cannot be transcribed uniquely from the printed layout without inventing a numerator or exponent.
Equation (16) has a visually unclear fraction/equality continuation and may not produce the claimed score direction.
Equation (17) prints a minimum with zero, which appears inconsistent with a nonnegative waste amount unless a sign convention is supplied.
Equation (19) has unstable exponent notation and no empirical calibration of its threshold or slope.
The prose calls Equation (22) inverse exponential while the printed expression appears to be a power function.
Table 5 mixes fitted, substituted, and experience-based values without parameter-specific provenance and uncertainty.
The four judgment matrices are presented without named assessors, elicitation protocol, disagreement handling, or uncertainty.
Matrix consistency and aggregation evidence are not reported alongside the weights.
The final score scale and aggregation choices are not validated against observed resident, ecological, or economic outcomes.
The body reports a selected strategy score of 0.6894 while the Summary reports improvement to 0.692; rounding or pipeline differences are not reconciled.
The reported 0.446 baseline and model score changes have no external decision threshold or uncertainty interval.
Morris screening lacks a complete reproducible specification of parameter ranges, trajectories, levels, seed, and treatment of interactions.
Large local sensitivities such as r1=792.18 and k5=575.2 depend on parameter units and evaluation point, so raw magnitudes are not directly comparable.
Global Morris and local derivative rankings are described together without explaining differences in scale, range, or interpretation.
Cliff retreat is substituted for glacier ELA, changing the physical mechanism while retaining the same state-equation form.
The Big Sur transfer reuses structure and coefficients without a full recalibration table, comparative fit metrics, or held-out validation.
The change 0.32773 to 0.73563 is model-generated and should not be phrased as observed improvement.
The 15,000-visitors-per-day cap is not derived transparently from the displayed optimization or an enforceable capacity constraint.
The memo's 40-percent environmental allocation does not visibly match the selected vector [0.15,0.10,0.35,0.10,0.30].
The claim of up to 30-percent annual glacier-degradation reduction lacks a displayed derivation and uncertainty interval.
Housing affordability and tax relief are recommended without a housing-market model, incidence analysis, eligibility rule, or distributional assessment.
The paper itself excludes heatwaves, pandemics, and other unexpected events, limiting robustness of the proposed policy.
The paper itself acknowledges that immediate policy effects ignore implementation delay and may bias forecasts.
Source names are listed, but a frozen data bundle, exact URLs, retrieval dates, transformations, and licenses are not provided.
No complete code, environment, data bundle, parameter file, seed, or single replay command is supplied.
Single-paper observations may inform source-specific evidence only; they do not establish a general MCM writing or modeling rule.

Check each data source, retrieval date, transformation, unit, proxy role, and downstream consumer.
Check dimensions, signs, climate confounding, and coefficient identifiability in Equation (1).
Check logistic-flow interpretation, carrying capacity, tax mechanism, and units in Equations (2)-(3).
Check 2013 exclusion, interpolation, fitting, residuals, and omega units in Equations (4)-(6).
Check allocation sums, budgets, policy coding, feasibility, and state-effect mappings.
Check score direction, range, normalization, units, and exact transcription for Equations (7)-(9).
Check ambiguous Equations (10)-(19), especially natural-resource, energy, waste, and carbon forms.
Check AHP assessors, matrix entries, CR, aggregation, double counting, and weight uncertainty.
Check selected-vector feasibility and reconcile 0.6894 with the Summary's 0.692.
Check Morris ranges, trajectories, levels, seed, and global-versus-local interpretation.
Check units and evaluation point before comparing local sensitivity magnitudes.
Check every Big Sur substitution, recalibrated coefficient, fit metric, holdout test, and score claim.
Check each memo number, owner, budget, trigger, monitoring measure, implementation delay, and evidence boundary against the body.

Equation (7) contains visually unstable arrows, exponents, and mu subscripts; its exact algebra must be checked against the source before reuse.
Equation (9) has unclear exponent signs and parameter placement, so the asserted normalization range is not independently established.
Equation (14) cannot be transcribed uniquely from the printed layout without inventing a numerator or exponent.
Equation (16) has a visually unclear fraction/equality continuation and may not produce the claimed score direction.
Equation (17) prints a minimum with zero, which appears inconsistent with a nonnegative waste amount unless a sign convention is supplied.
Equation (19) has unstable exponent notation and no empirical calibration of its threshold or slope.
The prose calls Equation (22) inverse exponential while the printed expression appears to be a power function.
Table 5 mixes fitted, substituted, and experience-based values without parameter-specific provenance and uncertainty.
The four judgment matrices are presented without named assessors, elicitation protocol, disagreement handling, or uncertainty.
Matrix consistency and aggregation evidence are not reported alongside the weights.
The final score scale and aggregation choices are not validated against observed resident, ecological, or economic outcomes.
The body reports a selected strategy score of 0.6894 while the Summary reports improvement to 0.692; rounding or pipeline differences are not reconciled.
The reported 0.446 baseline and model score changes have no external decision threshold or uncertainty interval.
Morris screening lacks a complete reproducible specification of parameter ranges, trajectories, levels, seed, and treatment of interactions.
Large local sensitivities such as r1=792.18 and k5=575.2 depend on parameter units and evaluation point, so raw magnitudes are not directly comparable.
Global Morris and local derivative rankings are described together without explaining differences in scale, range, or interpretation.
Cliff retreat is substituted for glacier ELA, changing the physical mechanism while retaining the same state-equation form.
The Big Sur transfer reuses structure and coefficients without a full recalibration table, comparative fit metrics, or held-out validation.
The change 0.32773 to 0.73563 is model-generated and should not be phrased as observed improvement.
The 15,000-visitors-per-day cap is not derived transparently from the displayed optimization or an enforceable capacity constraint.
The memo's 40-percent environmental allocation does not visibly match the selected vector [0.15,0.10,0.35,0.10,0.30].
The claim of up to 30-percent annual glacier-degradation reduction lacks a displayed derivation and uncertainty interval.
Housing affordability and tax relief are recommended without a housing-market model, incidence analysis, eligibility rule, or distributional assessment.
The paper itself excludes heatwaves, pandemics, and other unexpected events, limiting robustness of the proposed policy.
The paper itself acknowledges that immediate policy effects ignore implementation delay and may bias forecasts.
Source names are listed, but a frozen data bundle, exact URLs, retrieval dates, transformations, and licenses are not provided.
No complete code, environment, data bundle, parameter file, seed, or single replay command is supplied.
Single-paper observations may inform source-specific evidence only; they do not establish a general MCM writing or modeling rule.

writing_logic.summary: Summary: overtourism, H-N-T dynamics, interventions, AHP, Juneau scores, two sensitivity methods, and Big Sur transfer -> move from the dual challenge through state variables, intervention choice, evaluation, sensitivity, and transfer while binding each stage to a number -> compress the complete source argument before the memo and Contents -> a task-method-result-transfer ladder -> 1.1 Problem Background.

1.1 Problem Background: Juneau landscapes, cruise growth, environment, infrastructure, residents, visitor caps, and cruise agreements -> open with place and attraction, pivot with But to local harms, and end by declaring existing measures insufficient -> establish the location-specific benefit-pressure problem without the disclosed AI-assisted global paragraph -> a bounded Juneau motivation -> 1.2 Restatement.

1.2 Restatement and 1.3 Our Work: three official tasks, STDM, intervention combinations, AHP feedback, Juneau, Big Sur, sensitivity, and advice -> turn the task into three numbered obligations and then answer with a three-component system and a transfer plan -> align requirements with a visible method and output sequence -> an inspectable task-to-work contract -> 2 Assumptions.

2 Assumptions and Justifications: instant policy, absence of disasters, stable coefficients, and authoritative data -> state Assumption N and immediately explain its modeling convenience or consequence -> make simplifying premises explicit before notation and data -> a premise-rationale scope envelope -> 3 Notations.

3 Notations: Juneau and Big Sur states, intervention components, allocations, parameters, and score symbols -> freeze the shared vocabulary in Table 1 before data and equations -> type quantities shared by dynamics, scoring, transfer, and policy -> a cross-model symbol ledger -> 4 Model Preparation.

4 Model Preparation: missing predefined data, representative selection, named sources, and the population-environment-economy interface -> admit that listing everything is impractical, choose accurate representative data, and explain each H-N-T role -> turn an open data search into a bounded source-and-variable contract -> Table 2, H-N-T selections, and ELA construction -> 5 Model Design.

5.1 STDM and Glacier ELA Dynamics: Lotka-Volterra, logistic, SIS inspiration, tourist flow, glacier ELA, natural change, tourist pressure, and restoration -> introduce the coupled-system analogy, justify the environmental proxy term by term, then print Equation (1) -> construct the first state equation from named mechanisms -> the H_J environmental-state interface -> 5.1.2 Tourist Dynamics.

5.1.2-5.1.4 Tourist, Economic, and Integrated Dynamics: tourist carrying capacity, glacier attraction, hotel tax, nonlinear regression, and system integration -> define one state at a time, explain each coefficient in ordinary language, and hand separate equations into integration -> complete the three-state mechanism before intervention -> Equations (2)-(3) and the integration setup -> integrated system.

5.1.4 Integrated System and Projection Results: 2013 Blob exclusion, interpolation, fitted parameters, omega terms, and three-dimensional projections -> state the data exception, print Equations (4)-(6) together, then show the trajectory and pairwise projections -> connect preprocessing and intervention-ready dynamics to visual behavior -> an integrated STDM result block -> 5.2 Intervention Strategies.

5.1 Results and 5.2 Intervention Lead: trajectory projections, three qualitative insights, and the intervention-section handoff -> interpret the plots in a short numbered result sequence and announce intervention strategy -> turn simulated state behavior into the next decision stage -> three directional findings and an intervention handoff -> 5.2.2 Allocation.

5.2.2-6.1 Allocation, Policies, and Evaluation Factors: nine allocation arrays, eight policy vectors, state interventions, three evaluation factors, and selected indicators -> show candidate allocations and policy effects before opening the evaluation hierarchy -> convert a finite intervention set into scored alternatives -> allocation-policy candidates and the evaluation contract -> 6.1 Indicators.

6.1-6.2 Indicator Hierarchy and AHP Setup: 29 considered indicators, 12 selected indicators, LoR, EP, EDoS, pairwise comparison, consistency, and aggregation -> narrow a broad indicator pool, display the hierarchy, then define AHP before formula detail -> turn sustainability dimensions into a weighted score architecture -> a three-factor, twelve-indicator evaluation hierarchy -> resident indicators.

6.2 Resident Score Construction: income, crowding, housing, normalization, tax allocation, population density, and sigmoid response -> explain the intended mechanism before each displayed formula and name normalization afterward -> construct resident-welfare score components -> Equations (7)-(9) and their stated interpretations -> remaining resident and environmental scores.

6.2 Resident and Environmental Score Construction: housing, noise, natural resources, energy, waste, carbon, baselines, saturation, and allocations -> repeat label, mechanism, formula, and plain-language interpretation across six indicators -> complete resident and environmental score components while preserving printed ambiguity -> Equations (10)-(19) -> economic-development scores.

6.2-7 Development Scores, Parameters, Weights, and Factors: tax, employment, culture, safety, parameter substitution, AHP matrices, optimization factors, and constraints -> finish four indicators, explain experience-based parameter selection, then hand score construction to factor classification -> close evaluation definitions and prepare policy selection -> Equations (20)-(23), parameter and factor interfaces -> AHP matrices and constraints.

6.4-7 AHP Matrices and Factor Classification: four judgment matrices, CR checks, weights, optimized components, and constraint components -> show matrices and consistency values before dividing factors into objectives and constraints -> make score weights and optimization roles inspectable -> Table 5, Table 6, matrices, and factor roles -> 8 Results.

8 Results and Discussion: weight heatmap, fitted H-N-T comparisons, feasible intervention example, and interpretation -> place Figures 7 and 8 before a worked policy combination -> turn weights and fitted trajectories into a candidate decision -> an interpretable scored intervention example -> selected policy.

8 Results and 9.1 Morris Sensitivity: selected allocation, policy code, score 0.6894, baseline comparison, and Morris screening -> report the best combination, compare baseline and model scores, then open global screening -> connect policy selection to factor importance -> selected intervention, score comparison, and Morris setup -> 9.2 Local Sensitivity.

9.1-9.2 Global and Local Sensitivity: Morris elementary effects, ODE parameters, score parameters, local partial derivatives, and Table 7 -> interpret the two Morris panels before changing scale to local derivatives -> separate global range-based screening from pointwise sensitivity -> two sensitivity views and a ranked local table handoff -> 10 Big Sur.

9.2 and 10.1 Local Effects and Big Sur Foundations: Figure 11, overtourism site specificity, Big Sur context, park attendance, revenue, cliff retreat, and data aggregation -> rank local effects, pivot to a new destination, and define each transferred state from named data -> turn sensitivity closure into a destination-specific transfer interface -> a Big Sur H-N-T data contract -> 10.2 Transfer.

9.2 Table 7 and 10.1 Transfer Continuation: local sensitivity values, environmental substitution, tourist attendance, and revenue -> close sensitivity with a numeric table and resume transfer variable construction -> preserve scale-dependent local results before structural reuse -> Table 7 and Big Sur state definitions -> 10.2 Validity.

10.2 Big Sur Validity and Generalizability: normalized Big Sur states, transferred dynamics, least squares, state vector, and score change -> show the data-source visual, print the transferred system, fit, report the normalized state, and compare scores -> test structural portability with destination-specific proxies -> Equation (24), a state vector, and 0.32773-to-0.73563 result -> 11 Evaluation.

11.1 Strengths: comprehensiveness, dynamics, regional parameters, and quantitative policy scoring -> list four source-authored positive claims after transfer -> separate claimed advantages from independent evidence -> a bounded strengths register -> 11.2 Weaknesses.

11.2 Weaknesses: unexpected events and policy implementation delay -> state two limitations and name the mechanism by which they can bias results -> bound the paper's claims before references -> a repair-oriented limitation register -> Memorandum.

Memorandum: the Juneau Tourist Council, 1.6 million passengers, a 15,000 daily cap, 40-percent environmental allocation, resident housing relief, and claimed glacier benefit -> open with institutional context, move from urgency to two recommendations and resident consequences, and close with confidence and signature -> translate the model into council-facing actions and claims -> a one-page stakeholder memo -> source boundary.
